nameStory: Hairy Saltwort gets its name from two key features that help it survive in harsh conditions. The 'hairy' part comes from the fine, fuzzy hairs covering its stems and leaves, which help protect it from drying winds and intense sun. The 'saltwort' part refers to its ability to tolerate salty soils where many other plants can't grow, making it a specialist of challenging environments.
description: Hairy Saltwort is a small, scrubby annual plant that looks somewhat like a miniature tumbleweed. This hardy little survivor grows low to the ground with branching stems covered in tiny, narrow leaves that feel soft and fuzzy to the touch. It's a relatively small plant, typically staying under a foot tall, and has an overall bushy, rounded appearance when mature.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low, rounded, bushy clump with many branching stems radiating from the base, giving it a compact cushion-like appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, narrow leaves that feel distinctly soft and fuzzy due to dense, fine hairs covering the surface - run your finger along them and you'll notice the velvety texture

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous greenish flowers tucked among the leaves, lacking showy petals and easily overlooked without close inspection

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Multiple branching stems covered in the same soft, fine hairs as the leaves, giving the entire plant a grayish-green, fuzzy appearance

habitat: This is an extremely rare plant in New England, with only a single recorded observation in the region. When found, it would likely be in disturbed, sandy, or salty soils such as roadsides treated with winter salt, coastal areas, or other harsh, dry locations where few plants can establish.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, and young plants begin developing their characteristic fuzzy, branching stems.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their small, inconspicuous flowers hidden among the hairy leaves.
seasonality.fall: Plants set seed and may break away at the base, potentially rolling like small tumbleweeds to disperse seeds.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to wait for spring germination.

funFact: Hairy Saltwort is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only once in the entire region - making it one of the most elusive plants you could ever hope to find here, rarer than finding a needle in a haystack!
confusionNotes: Its small size and fuzzy appearance might remind you of some small chickweeds or other tiny weedy plants, but the distinctly soft, velvety texture of the narrow leaves and the overall rounded, cushion-like growth habit set it apart from other small roadside plants.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the Amaranth family, Hairy Saltwort looks nothing like the colorful garden amaranths or edible amaranth grains most people know - it's a completely different type of plant that happens to share the same botanical family tree.
compareHints: Hairy Saltwort is the only species in its genus Spirobassia, making it truly unique. Within the broader Amaranth family, it's much smaller and fuzzier than relatives like lamb's quarters or pigweed, and lacks the prominent flower spikes typical of most amaranths. Its compact, cushion-like form and intensely hairy texture make it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
